::: {.callout-tip}
#### Learning Objectives

- Know how to filter proteins for statistical testing based on quantification across replicates
- Using the `limma` package (@Smyth2004), design a statistical model with contrasts to test for differentially abundant proteins across multiple conditions
- Understand the F-test for overall significance across groups
- Interpret the results of individual pairwise contrasts and apply global multiple testing correction
- Produce volcano plots to visualise the results of differential abundance analysis
:::





## Differential abundance analysis

Having cleaned our data, log2 transformed it and aggregated from precursor to protein level, we are now ready to carry out statistical analysis.

The aim of this section is to answer the question: *"Which proteins show a significant change in abundance between MPXV-infected patients, COVID-19 patients, and healthy controls?"*.

Our null hypothesis is: **(H0)** The mean protein abundance is the same across all three groups.

Our alternative hypothesis is: **(H1)** The mean protein abundance differs between at least one pair of groups.

## Selecting a statistical test

There are a few aspects of our data that we need to consider prior to deciding which statistical test to apply.

- The protein abundances in this data are not normally distributed (i.e., they do not follow a Gaussian distribution).
  However, they are approximately normal following a log-transformation.
- We assume that the variance is approximately equal across the three groups.
- The samples are independent and not paired --- each patient contributes a single sample to one group only.

The first point relates to a key assumption of **Gaussian linear modelling**,
which assumes that the residuals (difference between the observed values and the
values predicted by the model) are Gaussian distributed. If this assumption is
not met, it is not appropriate to use a Gaussian linear model. For quantitative
proteomics data, it is reasonable to assume the residuals will be approximately
Gaussian distributed if we first log-transform the abundances.

Many different R packages can be used to carry out differential abundance
analysis on proteomics data. Here we will use `limma`, a package that is widely
used for omics analysis and can be used in single comparisons or multifactorial
experiments using an **empirical Bayes-moderated linear model**. A simple
example of the empirical Bayes-moderated linear model is provided in
@Hutchings2023.


### What does the empirical Bayes part mean?

When carrying out high throughput omics experiments we not only have a
population of samples but also a population of features - here we have
several thousand proteins. Proteomics experiments are typically lowly replicated
(e.g n < 10), therefore, the per-protein variance estimates are relatively
inaccurate. The empirical Bayes method borrows information across
features (proteins) and shifts the per-protein variance estimates
towards an expected value based on the variance estimates of other
proteins with a similar abundance. This improves the accuracy of the variance
estimates, thus reducing false negatives for proteins with over-estimated variance and reducing false positives from proteins with under-estimated variance. For more detail about the empirical Bayes methods, see
[here](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat555/node/40/).


## Handling missing values prior to testing

Label-free DIA data has many missing values at the protein level.
Before statistical testing, we need to decide how to handle proteins that are not quantified in enough samples within each group to support a reliable estimate of group-level abundance.

We only want to test proteins which are quantified in at least 3 replicates of each condition.

We begin by extracting the protein-level data `"proteins"` from
the QFeatures object. This contains all 282
proteins, before any filtering on replication.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
se <- getWithColData(dia_qf, "proteins")
print(se)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


:::
:::


For each group in turn, we count the number of non-missing values per protein and keep only proteins quantified in at least 3 samples of every group.
Looping over the groups means the same code works for any number of groups.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tokeep <- rep(TRUE, nrow(se))

for (g in unique(se$group)) {
  n_quantified <- rowSums(!is.na(assay(se[, se$group == g])))
  tokeep <- tokeep & n_quantified >= 3
}

print(table(tokeep))
```

:::


We now add a new set containing only the proteins that pass the replication
filter, and link it to the parent set. We see we are left with 
264 proteins to test.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dia_qf <- addAssay(dia_qf, y = se[tokeep, ], name = "proteins_replicated")

dia_qf <- addAssayLink(
  dia_qf,
  from = "proteins",
  to = "proteins_replicated"
)

```

## Defining the statistical model

We use `model.matrix` to define the design matrix for our linear model.
Since we have three groups and are interested in all pairwise comparisons, we use a model without an intercept (`~0 + group`).
This means the model estimates the mean abundance for each group directly.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
group <- factor(dia_qf$group, levels = c("control", "MPXV", "Covid19"))

limma_design <- model.matrix(formula(~ 0 + group))

# Rename design matrix columns to make them easier to refer to
colnames(limma_design) <- levels(group)

## Verify
limma_design
```

## Fitting the linear model

We fit the linear model to the replicated protein data using `lmFit`.
This estimates the mean abundance of each group for every protein.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data <- assay(dia_qf[['proteins_replicated']])

limma_fit <- lmFit(data, limma_design)
```
:::


## Defining contrasts and moderating the variances

A **contrast** is a comparison between group means that we want to test.
We are interested in all three pairwise comparisons between the groups.
The `makeContrasts` function creates a contrast matrix specifying how each difference between group means is calculated.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Specify contrasts of interest
contrasts_matrix <- makeContrasts(
  MPXV_control = MPXV - control,
  Covid19_control = Covid19 - control,
  MPXV_Covid19 = MPXV - Covid19,
  levels = limma_design
)

## Verify
contrasts_matrix
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
         Contrasts
Levels    MPXV_control Covid19_control MPXV_Covid19
  control           -1              -1            0
  MPXV               1               0            1
  Covid19            0               1           -1
```


:::
:::


We apply the contrasts to the fitted model and update it using the `eBayes` function with `trend = TRUE` and `robust = TRUE` to account for the intensity-dependent variance trend typical in quantitative proteomics data.

-   `trend` - takes a logical value of `TRUE` or `FALSE` to indicate
    whether an intensity-dependent trend should be allowed for the prior
    variance (i.e., the population level variance prior to empirical
    Bayes moderation). This means that when the empirical Bayes
    moderation is applied the protein variances are not squeezed towards
    a global mean but rather towards an intensity-dependent trend.
-   `robust` - takes a logical value of `TRUE` or `FALSE` to indicate
    whether the parameter estimation of the priors should be robust
    against outlier sample variances.

See (@Phipson2016 and @Smyth2004) for further details.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
limma_fit_contrasts <- contrasts.fit(
  fit = limma_fit,
  contrasts = contrasts_matrix
)

limma_fit_contrasts <- eBayes(limma_fit_contrasts, trend = TRUE, robust = TRUE)
```
:::


All of the results in this lesson, the F-test and each pairwise comparison, are extracted from this one fit using `topTable`.

### Diagnostic plots to verify suitability of our statistical model

As with all statistical analysis, it is crucial to do some quality
control and to check that the statistical test that has been applied was
indeed appropriate for the data. As mentioned above, statistical tests
typically come with several assumptions. To check that these assumptions
were met and that our model was suitable, we create some diagnostic
plots.

The first plot that we generate is an SA plot to display the residual
standard deviation (sigma) versus log abundance for each protein to
which our model was fitted. We can use the `plotSA` function to do this.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plotSA(fit = limma_fit_contrasts, cex = 0.5, xlab = "Average log2 abundance")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06_statistical_analysis_files/figure-html/plot-sa-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


It is recommended that an SA plot be used as a routine diagnostic plot
when applying a limma-trend pipeline. From the SA plot we can visualise
the intensity-dependent trend that has been incorporated into our
linear model. It is important to verify that the trend line fits the
data well. If we had not included the `trend = TRUE` argument in our
`eBayes` function, then we would instead see a straight horizontal line
that does not follow the trend of the data. Further, the plot also
colours any outliers in red. These are the outliers that are only
detected and excluded when using the `robust = TRUE` argument.

Next, we plot a histogram of the raw p-values (not adjusted
p-values). This can be done by passing our results data into standard
`ggplot2` plotting functions.

The near-flat distribution across the bottom corresponds to
null p-values which are distributed approximately uniformly between 0
and 1. The peak close to 0 contains a combination of our significantly changing proteins (true positives) and proteins with a low p-value by chance (false positives).

Other examples of how a p-value histogram could look are shown below.
Whilst in some experiments a uniform p-value distribution may arise due
to an absence of significant alternative hypotheses, other distribution
shapes can indicate that something was wrong with the model design or
statistical test. For more detail on how to interpret p-value histograms
there is a great
[blog post](http://varianceexplained.org/statistics/interpreting-pvalue-histogram/)
by David Robinson, from which the examples below are taken.



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Examples of p-value histograms.](../_shared/figs/phist_shapes.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Recognising a poorly behaved SA plot

{{< level 2 >}}

The SA plots below were drawn from the same protein-level data as our model.
The left panel is our analysis.
In the other two panels, values were removed or replaced before the model was refitted with the same `eBayes(trend = TRUE, robust = TRUE)` settings.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![SA plots for our analysis (left), after the lowest 10% of values were removed and imputed with `MinDet` (middle) and after 10% of values were removed at random and replaced by zero (right).](../_shared/figs/sa_plot_examples.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


1. How does the trend line in each of the other two panels differ from the trend line in ours?
2. Where do the red outlier proteins sit in each panel, and what do they tell us about those proteins?
3. If you saw a plot like the middle or right panel for your own data, what would you check first?

::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
Our trend line is close to flat, and the proteins scatter evenly around it across the whole abundance range.

In the middle panel the trend line falls steeply at the lowest abundances, and the red outliers sit at the very left edge with a residual standard deviation much smaller than the other proteins.
`MinDet` replaces the missing values in each sample with a single low value, so the imputed values in a protein are almost identical to each other and its variance is artificially small.

In the right panel the whole cloud moves up to a residual standard deviation of around 2, and the proteins extend down to much lower average abundances than in the other panels.
A zero on the log2 scale is far below any measured abundance, so each imputed zero adds a large artificial variance to its protein.
The red outliers are proteins whose variance is far below the trend.

In both cases the variance of many proteins reflects the imputation rather than the measurements.
We would check how many values were imputed, whether they are concentrated in a few samples or proteins, and whether the imputed values are plausible for the abundance range of the data.
:::::
:::

## F-test for overall significance across groups

::: callout-note

### What is an F-value?

An F-value is a parametric statistical value used to compare the mean
values of **three or more** groups. The F-value is the ratio of the between-group
variation (explained variance) and the within-group variance (unexplained variance).
The higher the F-value, the more significant the difference between the groups is.
:::


We first ask whether a protein differs between *any* of the three groups, using an F-test.
In `limma`, the F-test tests whether all of the contrasts in the fit are zero at the same time.
The MPXV versus Covid19 contrast is the difference between the other two, so it adds no information to the F-test, which is based on the two independent comparisons among three groups.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Experiments with two groups

With two groups there is only one contrast, and the F-test is the same as the moderated t-test for that contrast (the F-statistic is the square of the t-statistic).
In that case this step can be skipped and the analysis can go straight to the pairwise results below.
:::

Setting `coef = NULL` in `topTable` returns the F-statistic for each protein, which tests the null hypothesis that the mean abundance is equal across all groups.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Format results
limma_results_F <- topTable(
  fit = limma_fit_contrasts,
  coef = NULL,
  adjust.method = "BH", # Method for multiple hypothesis testing
  number = Inf
) %>% # Print results for all proteins
  rownames_to_column("UniprotID")

head(limma_results_F)
```

#### Challenge: Interpreting the F-test p-value distribution

{{< level 2 >}}

Using `limma_results_F`, plot a histogram of the raw F-test p-values (`P.Value`) and compare it with the example p-value histograms above.

1. Does the distribution match what you would expect if many proteins are truly differentially abundant?
2. Is there anything in its shape that suggests a problem with the model?
3. What does a small F-test p-value tell us about a protein, and what does it not tell us?
4. How could we find out which groups differ?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>`ggplot(limma_results_F, aes(x = P.Value)) + geom_histogram()` is a good starting point.</details>

::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
limma_results_F %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = P.Value)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_classic() +
  ggtitle("Distribution of p-values for F-test")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06_statistical_analysis_files/figure-html/f-test-pvalue-histogram-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The histogram has a sharp peak close to 0 and a lower, roughly flat distribution across the rest of the range.
This is the shape expected when many proteins truly differ and the remaining proteins follow the null.
There is no sign of a problem such as a peak near 1 or a U shape.

A small F-test p-value tells us that the mean abundance of at least one group differs from the others.
It does not tell us which groups differ, in which direction, or by how much.
To find out, we test the individual pairwise comparisons using t-tests on the contrasts.
:::::
:::

## Pairwise contrasts

The F-test identifies proteins that differ somewhere across the groups.
To find out which groups differ and in which direction, we extract the moderated t-test results for each pairwise contrast from the same fit.

::: callout-note

### What is a t-value?

A t-value is a parametric statistical value used to compare the mean
values of **two** groups. The t-value is the ratio of the difference in means to
the standard error of the difference in means. The further away from zero that a
t-value lies, the more significant the difference between the groups is.
:::

::: callout-note

### How is the p-value obtained?

A p-value may be obtained from a t-value/F-value by comparing the value against
a t-value/F-distribution with the appropriate degrees of freedom.

-   **degrees of freedom** = the number of observations minus the number
    of independent variables in the model
-   **p-value** = the probability of achieving the t-value/F-value under the
    null hypothesis i.e., by chance

:::


We start by extracting results for a single contrast, MPXV versus control.
We use `topTable` with `coef = "MPXV_control"` to get the results for this specific comparison.
We also merge in gene name annotations from the `rowData`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
limma_results_mpxv_control <- topTable(
  limma_fit_contrasts,
  coef = "MPXV_control",
  number = Inf,
  sort.by = "p"
) %>%
  data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column('UniprotID')

uniprot_annotations <- rowData(dia_qf[['proteins_replicated']]) %>%
  data.frame() %>%
  select(Genes, Protein.Names)

limma_results_mpxv_control <- limma_results_mpxv_control %>%
  merge(uniprot_annotations, by.x = 'UniprotID', by.y = 'row.names') %>%
  arrange(P.Value)

limma_results_mpxv_control %>%
  ggplot(aes(P.Value)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_classic() +
  ggtitle("P-value distribution for MPXV vs Control contrast")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.
```

How many significant changes in abundance are there?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
table(
  sig = limma_results_mpxv_control$adj.P.Val < 0.05,
  ifelse(limma_results_mpxv_control$logFC > 0, 'Increased', 'Decreased')
)
```

### Multiple hypothesis testing and correction

Using the linear model defined above, we have carried out a
statistical test for each protein.

Multiple testing describes the process of separately testing multiple null
hypothesis i.e., carrying out many statistical tests at a time, each to
test a null hypothesis on different data. Here we have carried out
one statistical test per protein.
If we were to use the typical p \< 0.05 significance threshold for each
test, we would expect a 5% chance of incorrectly rejecting the null
hypothesis *per test*. For a typical proteomics dataset with thousands of
proteins, we would expect many p-values <= 0.05 by chance.

If we do not account for the fact that we have carried out multiple
hypothesis, we risk including false positives in our data. Many
methods exist to correct for multiple hypothesis testing and these
mainly fall into two categories:

1.  Control of the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER)
2.  Control of the False Discovery Rate (FDR)

Above we specified the "BH" method for adjusting p-values in our `topTable` function call. This is shorthand for the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, to control the FDR.

::: callout-tip
#### The False Discovery Rate

The False Discovery Rate (FDR) defines the fraction of false discoveries
that we are willing to tolerate in our list of differential proteins.
For example, an FDR threshold of 0.05 means that approximately 5% of the
proteins deemed differentially abundant will be false positives. It is up to you
to decide what this threshold should be, but conventionally a value between 0.01
(1% FPs) and 0.1 (10% FPs) is chosen.
:::


## Visualising results: the volcano plot

The final step in any statistical analysis is to visualise the results.
This is important for ourselves as it allows us to check that the data
looks as expected.

The most common visualisation used to display the results of expression
proteomics experiments is a volcano plot. This is a scatterplot that
shows statistical significance (p-values) against the magnitude of fold
change. Of note, when we plot the statistical significance we use the
raw unadjusted p-value (`-log10(P.Value)`). This is because it is better
to plot the statistical test results in their 'raw' form and not values derived from them (the
adjusted p-value is derived from each p-value using the BH-method of
correction). Furthermore, the process of FDR correction can result in some points
that previously had distinct p-values having the same adjusted p-value.
Finally, different methods of correction will generate different
adjusted p-values, making the comparison and interpretation of values
more difficult.


::: {.callout-discussion}
#### Discussion

- What information does a volcano plot convey, and what are its limitations?
- Why might some proteins have a large fold change but not be statistically significant?
- Look at the proteins near the significance threshold --- what does this tell you about treating `adj.P.Val < 0.05` as a hard cut-off?
:::

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
Each point shows a protein's estimated change (x axis) against the strength of evidence for that change (y axis).
The plot does not show the protein's abundance, how many samples it was quantified in, or the uncertainty on its fold change.
The y axis shows the raw p-value, while the colour uses the adjusted p-value.

A large fold change can fail to reach significance when the protein varies a lot between samples, is quantified in few samples, or sits at low abundance where the variance trend is high.
In MPXV vs control, 4 proteins have a fold change greater than 2 but are not significant.

25 proteins have adjusted p-values between 0.03 and 0.08.
The evidence for a protein at 0.04 is hardly different from the evidence for one at 0.06.
The cut-off is a convenience for reporting, and ranking proteins or reading the evidence as continuous describes the result better.
:::

We produce a volcano plot for the MPXV vs Control contrast, labelling the top 30 most significant proteins by gene name.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data_for_highlighting <- limma_results_mpxv_control %>%
  filter(adj.P.Val < 0.05) %>%
  arrange(P.Value) %>%
  head(30)

ggplot(
  limma_results_mpxv_control,
  aes(
    logFC,
    -log10(P.Value),
    colour = adj.P.Val < 0.05,
    alpha = adj.P.Val < 0.05
  )
) +
  geom_point(pch = 20, size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = data_for_highlighting,
    aes(label = Genes),
    vjust = 1.5,
    size = 2,
    colour = 'grey20'
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  xlab("Log2 Fold Change (MPXV vs Control)") +
  ylab("-Log10 P-value") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c('grey', 'orangered3')) +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(0.2, 1)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Extracting results for all contrasts

Rather than extracting results for each contrast separately, we can loop through all contrasts and bind the results into a single long-format data frame.
This format is well-suited for downstream visualisation with `ggplot2`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
contrasts <- colnames(contrasts_matrix)

limma_results_all_contrasts_list <- vector('list', length(contrasts))
names(limma_results_all_contrasts_list) <- contrasts

for (contrast in contrasts) {
  limma_results_all_contrasts_list[[contrast]] <- topTable(
    limma_fit_contrasts,
    coef = contrast,
    number = Inf,
    sort.by = "p"
  ) %>%
    data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column('UniprotID') %>%
    merge(uniprot_annotations, by.x = 'UniprotID', by.y = 'row.names') %>%
    mutate(contrast = contrast) %>%
    arrange(P.Value)
}
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# bind into one data.frame
limma_results_all_contrasts <- bind_rows(limma_results_all_contrasts_list)
```
:::


### Inspecting p-value distributions across contrasts

::: {.callout-discussion}
#### Discussion

- Before interpreting the results in detail, what can you infer just from the shape of the p-value distributions across the three contrasts?
- Which contrast shows the strongest signal, and what does that suggest about the biology?
:::

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}


If no protein changed, the histograms would be flat, with about 5% of p-values below 0.05.
COVID-19 vs control and MPXV vs control both have a large peak near zero, with 36% and 34% of p-values below 0.05, so many proteins differ between infected patients and controls.
MPXV vs COVID-19 is close to flat (8% below 0.05), so few proteins differ between the two infections.

COVID-19 vs control shows the strongest signal, and the two infections appear to share much of their effect on the plasma proteome.
Group size matters too: there are 15 control, 10 COVID-19 and 6 MPXV samples.
The contrasts involving MPXV have less power, and MPXV vs COVID-19 compares the two smallest groups, so its flat histogram partly reflects power.
:::


::: {.cell}

### Global multiple testing correction across contrasts

::: {.callout-discussion}
#### Discussion

- Why do we need to adjust p-values when testing hundreds of proteins across multiple contrasts?
- What is the difference between adjusting each contrast separately versus adjusting globally across all contrasts and proteins?
- Which approach is more conservative, and in what circumstances might that matter?
:::

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
We run 792 tests (264 proteins in each of 3 contrasts).
If no protein changed, a threshold of p < 0.05 would still give about 40 false positives.

Adjusting each contrast separately controls the false discovery rate within each contrast's list of proteins.
Adjusting globally controls it across the combined list from all contrasts.

Neither approach is always the more conservative.
The `adj.P.Val` column from `topTable` is still adjusted within each contrast, so we can compare the two directly:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
limma_results_all_contrasts %>%
  mutate(adj_global = p.adjust(P.Value, method = "BH")) %>%
  group_by(contrast) %>%
  summarise(
    sig_per_contrast = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05),
    sig_global = sum(adj_global < 0.05)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  contrast        sig_per_contrast sig_global
  <chr>                      <int>      <int>
1 Covid19_control               73         62
2 MPXV_Covid19                   0          3
3 MPXV_control                  50         48
```


:::
:::


The Benjamini-Hochberg threshold depends on how many small p-values are in the pool being adjusted.
A contrast with few small p-values, pooled with two that have many, gets a more lenient threshold than it would on its own.
This matters when one contrast has little signal, since its hits under global adjustment rely on the signal in the other contrasts, and when a contrast is later reported on its own.
:::

When testing hundreds of proteins across multiple contrasts, p-values must be adjusted for multiple testing.
The standard Benjamini-Hochberg method was designed for independent tests, but our contrasts share data and are positively correlated.
BH remains valid under positive dependence between tests, which is the kind expected between contrasts that share a control group, so we apply it once across all contrasts.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
limma_results_all_contrasts <- limma_results_all_contrasts %>%
  mutate(adj.P.Val = p.adjust(P.Value, method = 'BH'))
```
:::


This overwrites the `adj.P.Val` column, which `topTable` had adjusted within each contrast, with values adjusted across all contrasts together.
The number of significant MPXV vs control proteins below can therefore differ from the number in the MPXV vs control table above.

How many significant changes in abundance are there in each contrast?

::: {.callout-discussion}
#### Discussion

- Looking at the counts of significantly increased and decreased proteins across the three contrasts, what does this tell you about the differences between the conditions?
- Are you surprised by any of these numbers?
  What biological explanations might account for what you see?
:::

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}


COVID-19 vs control has 62 significant proteins (26 increased, 36 decreased) and MPXV vs control has 48 (24 increased, 24 decreased).
MPXV vs COVID-19 has 3.
Both infections change the plasma proteome relative to controls, in both directions, while the two infections barely differ from each other.

Part of the difference between the COVID-19 and MPXV counts is power, since there are only 6 MPXV samples.
A response common to infection, such as changes in proteins secreted into plasma during inflammation, would produce this pattern.
The scatter plot of fold changes in the next lesson shows whether the same proteins change in both infections.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
)
```

```
significant FALSE TRUE
```

:::
:::


The table gives the number of proteins in each combination of significance and fold-change threshold.
The two criteria measure different things: the adjusted p-value reflects how well the difference is supported by the data given the variability and the number of replicates, whereas the fold-change threshold reflects only the size of the estimated difference.
Proteins can therefore be significant with a small fold change, or have a large fold change without being significant.

The fold change is a point estimate and the plot shows no error on it.
A protein just outside a line may have an estimate that is within error of the threshold, so whether it truly exceeds a 2-fold change is uncertain.
A protein far outside the line is more likely to exceed it, but a large estimate is not by itself evidence of a reliable one.
The p-value is the only measure of uncertainty on the plot, and it tests whether the fold change differs from zero, not whether it exceeds 2-fold.
Testing against a fold-change threshold directly is the aim of the next exercise.
:::::
:::

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Using `treat` to test against a fold-change threshold

{{< level 2 >}}

The `eBayes` function tests the null hypothesis that a protein's log fold change is exactly zero.
In practice, we are often only interested in changes that exceed a minimum biologically meaningful fold change.
The `treat` function from `limma` instead tests the null hypothesis that the absolute log fold change is *less than* a specified threshold `fc`, providing a statistically rigorous alternative to post-hoc fold-change filtering.

1. Replace the `eBayes` call with `treat(fc=1.2, trend = TRUE, robust = TRUE)` and extract results for all contrasts using `topTreat` in place of `topTable`.
2. Apply global Benjamini-Hochberg correction to the p-values as before.
3. How many proteins are significant (`adj.P.Val < 0.05`) in each contrast compared to the `eBayes` results?
   Why is the number lower?

::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
limma_fit_treat <- treat(
  limma_fit_contrasts,
  fc = 1.2,
  trend = TRUE,
  robust = TRUE
)

limma_results_treat_list <- vector('list', length(contrasts))
names(limma_results_treat_list) <- contrasts

for (contrast in contrasts) {
  limma_results_treat_list[[contrast]] <- topTreat(
    limma_fit_treat,
    coef = contrast,
    n = Inf
  ) %>%
    rownames_to_column("UniprotID") %>%
    mutate(contrast = contrast)
}

limma_results_treat_all <- bind_rows(limma_results_treat_list) %>%
  mutate(adj.P.Val = p.adjust(P.Value, method = 'BH'))

table(
  sig = limma_results_treat_all$adj.P.Val < 0.05,
  limma_results_treat_all$contrast
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
       
sig     Covid19_control MPXV_control MPXV_Covid19
  FALSE             243          250          264
  TRUE               21           14            0
```


:::
:::


`treat` tests a stricter null hypothesis --- that the fold change is smaller than `fc = 1.2` (i.e. less than 1.2-fold) --- rather than simply that it is zero.
A protein must therefore show both statistical significance *and* a fold change exceeding the threshold to be called significant.
This reduces the number of hits compared to `eBayes`, retaining only those changes that are both statistically and practically meaningful.
:::::
:::





::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

- Before statistical testing, proteins should be filtered to those quantified in a minimum number of replicates per group to ensure reliable group-level abundance estimates
- When comparing more than two groups, a no-intercept design matrix (`~0 + group`) combined with contrasts provides a flexible way to specify all pairwise comparisons of interest
- The F-test (`coef = NULL` in `topTable`) tests for any significant difference across all groups simultaneously, before examining specific pairwise contrasts
- When testing multiple contrasts simultaneously, p-values should be adjusted globally across all proteins and contrasts to avoid inflated false positive rates; Benjamini-Hochberg correction is valid under the positive correlation structure typical of multi-contrast proteomics experiments
- Volcano plots are a useful summary of differential abundance results, but it is important to interpret them as one representation of a continuous statistical landscape rather than a binary significant/not-significant classification
:::
